transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-10-16
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Mateo Ruiz (Redwood SE), Asha Iyer (Redwood CSM); Priya Nair (MarlinForge CTO), Ethan Cole (Lead ML Eng), Jin Park (Infra), Samir Das (Product)
Recording ID: ff-20251016-marlinforge-01

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- MarlinForge is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for a low-latency inference product for their realtime assistant feature. Target p95 is 120-180ms for short streaming responses and ~350ms for longer dialog turns.
- Key constraints: token/sec bursts up to 1,200 tokens/sec aggregate, sustained concurrency ~200 streaming sessions, SOC2 + customer-managed KMS for PII, US + EU data residency.
- Action items: Redwood to send benchmark config and propose Dedicated pool sizing; customer to share token traces and representative prompt set.

Topics:
- Current infra and stack
- p95 latency targets & definitions (frontend vs end-to-end)
- Streaming behavior and token/sec burst patterns
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (SLA, cost, isolation)
- Security: SOC2, KMS, VPC options, audit logs
- Benchmark plan and next steps

Action Items (extracted):
- Lena to send benchmark config + pricing sheet (2025-10-20)
- Mateo to propose Dedicated sizing (2025-10-22)
- Ethan to share traces (2025-10-18)

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Lena (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick roll call?
[00:00:07] Priya (MarlinForge CTO): hi, Priya here, Ethan, Jin and Samir on my side.
[00:00:12] Ethan (MarlinForge): Ethan - lead on the ML infra stuff. 
[00:00:17] Mateo (Redwood SE): Mateo on the call, I'll be driving the latency/throughput bits.
[00:00:22] Jin (MarlinForge): Jin - infra, networking and onprem questions. audio is a bit rough on my end.
[00:00:30] Lena: awesome. quick context from us: Redwood offers hosted api, dedicated pools, and private deploys — same API surface. goal today is to understand your p95 targets, concurrency, streaming load, and any compliance needs that affect hosting.
[00:00:45] Priya: great. high level: our assistant has two main modes. quick completion replies (short prompts, streaming token bursts) and longer multi-turn generative steps used in knowledge retrieval. SLA target that leadership gave us is p95 under 180ms for the quick path, ideally 120ms. for long turns we can accept up to 350ms p95.
[00:01:10] Lena: ok that helps. when you say p95 are you measuring from your frontend to the user's first rendered token, or end-to-end including our runtime and network and client-side processing?
[00:01:21] Priya: good question. that's frontend-to-first-token. we have separate latency budget for network hop, so Redwood needs to ideally be ~120-140ms to leave us wiggle room.
[00:01:33] Ethan: also important: concurrency. we expect about 150-200 concurrent streaming sessions during peak, each session averaging 7-12 tokens/sec during the quick replies but then burst to 60-80 tokens/sec for a 2-3s window when the assistant outputs. aggregate burst we've seen up to 1,200 tokens/sec across region.
[00:01:55] Mateo: good, that's the kind of distribution we need to simulate. is that per region? US-east primarily, but we want failover to EU-west.
[00:02:04] Jin: yes primary US-east, but EU failover. also we need data residency—EU requests should stay in region.
[00:02:11] Asha (Redwood CSM): noted. on compliance - are you SOC2/ISO requirements internal or customer-driven?
[00:02:18] Priya: both. we already have SOC2 Type II and need vendors to have SOC2 or equivalent attestation. plus we want option for customer-managed KMS for sensitive PII vectors.
[00:02:29] Lena: Redwood supports SOC2 and we can integrate with customer KMS in Dedicated/Private modes; hosted has an optional KMS integration but the dedicated route is the most straightforward for full control.
[00:02:40] Samir (MarlinForge): on pricing, just to surface: our finance will prefer usage-based if cost-effective, but leadership may sign up for reserved Dedicated capacity if it ensures p95 and predictable costs.
[00:02:51] Mateo: that's the classic tradeoff — cost vs SLAs. we can show rough cost curves once we know QPS and token profiles.
[00:02:58] Ethan: can you explain prefix/K V cache? we saw that in your docs but not sure how it affects streaming latency.
[00:03:06] Mateo: yes. the prefix/KV cache stores key/value attention states for repeated prompt prefixes. for conversation style where users have repeated context, caching can eliminate recomputation and cut per-token latency significantly, especially for multi-turn where only new tokens are processed. for streaming the first token still has to compute a bit but subsequent tokens come out faster. it's workload dependent.
[00:03:27] Priya: our assistant uses a 512 token context, many prompts reuse a 250 token system prompt. sounds promising.
[00:03:33] Lena: do you quantize models in-house? any requirement for int8 or use of bfloat16?
[00:03:39] Ethan: we currently run mixed precision bfloat16 offline; for serving we'd prefer a quantized variant for cost reasons but worried about quality regressions.
[00:03:48] Mateo: we do recommend doing evals against your prompt suite. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and we can run an A/B canary to measure quality delta. typical drop for top open models is a small fraction, but depends on model.
[00:03:59] Jin: network wise: VPC peering is required for private deployment. what's the typical overhead for VPC private path vs hosted public endpoint?
[00:04:08] Mateo: VPC adds a few ms due to routing and security appliances; usually within 10-30ms depending on your network. but the benefit is private networking and control. for tight p95 you need to account for that in budget.
[00:04:18] Samir: okay, hypotheticals — if we target 120ms p95 for quick path, what hosting mode do you see as most realistic?
[00:04:25] Mateo: if you need strict p95 in single-digit region variance, Dedicated in-region pools give the best predictability. Hosted can meet it for many workloads but depends on shared tenancy, routing, and burst patterns. Private on-prem can get you lowest network hops but requires ops overhead.
[00:04:39] Priya: any numbers you can share for token/sec per GPU for the 7B-ish models? we plan to start with a distilled 7B and potentially move to a 13B later.
[00:04:49] Mateo: rough ballpark — for a quantized 7B on modern A100-like hardware you might see 2,000-3,500 tokens/sec per GPU in steady streaming generation for short sequences; for 13B it's often 700-1,200 tokens/sec depending on optimizations. but these vary a lot with decode parameters (top-k, temperature), seq length, and whether KV cache hits.
[00:05:08] Ethan: so our burst of 1,200 tokens/sec could be handled by a single 7B GPU in the best case — but concurrency and tail p95 matter.
[00:05:16] Mateo: exactly — steady tokens/sec is one metric, but p95 for first token and early tokens during bursts is shaped by batching and scheduling. Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching but can prioritize low-latency requests, and we have controls for max-batch and latency SLO enforcement.
[00:05:32] Priya: do you support model variants or multiple routed tiers? we may want a cheaper fallback model during heavy load.
[00:05:38] Lena: yes we support smart routing and fallbacks — policy-based. you can route to a compatible quantized variant or smaller model under load.
[00:05:45] Jin: curious about warm vs cold KV cache. if someone hasn't talked to the assistant in a while, cold start penalties?
[00:05:51] Mateo: cold starts affect first few tokens; caching strategies plus prefilling frequently used prompts can mitigate, but yes cold sessions have higher latency. Dedicated pools with reserved capacity reduce cold start frequency.
[00:06:05] Priya: ok let's talk benchmarking. what do you need from us to run a realistic token/sec and p95 test?
[00:06:11] Mateo: ideally: 1) sample prompts representative of both quick and long paths (about 30-50 prompts total), 2) token/sec traces by minute for the last 2 weeks to show burstiness, 3) target concurrency & p95 goals, and 4) any network topology constraints (VPC, IP allow lists).
[00:06:26] Ethan: we can provide that. last question: are you able to stream partial tokens or do you flush after full tokens? we're seeing jitter in some providers.
[00:06:34] Mateo: we stream partial tokens (server-side chunks) and support client-side SSE/websocket streaming; jitter often comes from client buffer or network. Redwood has observability hooks per-token and per-request tracing.
[00:06:46] Samir: you mentioned rollout strategies earlier — can you do canary by user segment?
[00:06:51] Lena: yes, rollouts support canary by header, user id hash, or percentage; you can also do A/B with automatic rollback if quality regressions detected.
[00:06:58] Priya: security specifics — do you log tokens? and do you provide redaction?
[00:07:04] Asha: default hosting logs usage metadata and non-reversible hashes of prompts for cost/analytics; dedicated/private options include configurable logging and optional token redaction. we can support minimal logs for regulated workloads.
[00:07:16] Priya: good. KMS — we need to ensure we can bring our key and rotate.
[00:07:20] Lena: yes bring-your-own-key supported for Dedicated and Private; hosted has an integration path with customer KMS but there are extra compliance steps. we'll include that in the security doc.
[00:07:29] Ethan: let's try to get concrete on sizing. can you walk through an example calculation for our 200 concurrent streaming sessions and bursts?
[00:07:36] Mateo: sure. scenario: 200 concurrent streaming sessions, average 10 tokens/sec steady, but assume 25% of sessions burst to 80 tokens/sec for 3 seconds every 30s. approximate aggregate steady tokens/sec ~2,000, burst aggregate peak ~ (150*10 + 50*80) = 1,500 + 4,000 = 5,500 tokens/sec during short windows. that's a heavy peak.
[00:08:00] Jin: 5,500 peak — that seems higher than our earlier 1,200 number; our logs vary a lot across days — we'll send traces.
[00:08:07] Mateo: right, that's why token traces are critical. for capacity we plan for steady-state plus an allowance for peaks; Dedicated sizing often reserves GPUs to keep p95 predictable, plus burst buffers (burst capacity) or autoscaling.
[00:08:20] Lena: operationally, Redwood Dedicated can set a reserved pool sized for steady state and autoscale with capped burst lanes to handle peaks. we can also set a fallback policy to cheaper models to reduce cost under extreme surges.
[00:08:32] Priya: what about multi-region replication and cross-region cold start? if EU failover kicks in, cold sessions might spike.
[00:08:39] Mateo: we recommend regional active-active with traffic steering; on failover, there's an inevitable transient spike — we model that during bench runs and can size warm standby capacity.
[00:08:49] Samir: are there examples of customers with similar p95 targets? not to ask for names, but ballpark architectures?
[00:08:55] Mateo: we've onboarded fintech and health customers with p95 in the 100-200ms range using Dedicated in-region pools, aggressive KV caching, and per-token prioritization.
[00:09:05] Ethan: ok, concrete bench plan then — can you send a config we can run in our environment to mirror your bench?
[00:09:11] Lena: yes we'll share a benchmark config, and you can run a smoke test and then we can run a hosted vs dedicated comparison with the same prompts.
[00:09:18] Jin: can you also include network emulation to replicate our WAN latency?
[00:09:22] Mateo: we can include a WAN-shaping profile. include your median and p95 network latency and we'll reproduce it.
[00:09:29] Priya: internal stakeholders will want a short document that maps latency budgets end-to-end. can you produce a one-pager we can use?
[00:09:36] Lena: yes we'll draft an E2E latency budget doc that shows allowances for client, network, and server.
[00:09:41] Priya: perfect. anything else on the compliance side?
[00:09:44] Asha: we'll attach our SOC2 attestation and security questionnaire. also include KMS integration notes for Dedicated/Private.
[00:09:52] Samir: switching topics — cost ballpark for Dedicated: if we reserve for steady-state tokens and have burst capacity, how do you model cost?
[00:09:59] Mateo: typically a hybrid: reserved monthly for baseline GPUs (committed) + overage for bursts or autoscale. we'll produce a cost curve once you share token traces and runbench.
[00:10:08] Priya: can Redwood run a pilot where we route a small percentage of production to your hosted endpoint first?
[00:10:14] Lena: yes that's common — a pilot traffic split (5-10%) to collect real-world latency and quality. we also instrument token-level tracing for the pilot.
[00:10:22] Ethan: timeline — we want the pilot in 2-3 weeks if possible.
[00:10:26] Lena: sounds doable if you share traces and prompts this week. we'll align the bench config and pricing.
[00:10:32] Jin: one more infra Q: do you support fixed IP ranges for allowlists?
[00:10:36] Asha: yes, for Dedicated we can provide static egress IPs; for hosted we have published ranges but they change, so dedicated is better for strict allowlists.
[00:10:44] Samir: ok let's move to Q&A from our side, Ethan — you had a question on p95 measurement?
[00:10:49] Ethan: yeah, how do you instrument p95 on your side to make it comparable to our frontend metrics?
[00:10:54] Mateo: we emit per-request timing: request receive, model decode first-token time, per-token deltas, and response close. we can provide a mapping guide to align our metrics with frontend-to-first-render. we'll include sample dashboards.
[00:11:07] Priya: in the bench, can you simulate user think-time and jitter?
[00:11:11] Mateo: yes bench configs include think-time distributions and token generation variability.
[00:11:16] Lena: quick note — sometimes our auto transcripts call things like K V cache as "K V" spelled out; apologies if any terms are off in the recording.
[00:11:24] (small cross-talk, background noise)
[00:11:40] Speaker 1 (intern): sorry if audio cuts — question, do you have a standard SLA template we can review?
[00:11:46] Lena: yes we'll send the SLA template, but for enterprise Dedicated/Private we do contract-level SLOs and uptime commitments.
[00:11:54] Priya: let's talk failure modes — if a node goes down during a burst, how do you maintain p95?
[00:11:59] Mateo: we have a couple strategies: 1) maintain headroom in pools, 2) have warm standby capacity for autoscale, 3) automated fallback to smaller model to preserve latency, 4) regional failover. most important is to plan for N+1 redundancy in Dedicated.
[00:12:15] Jin: what are your typical cold-cache p95 numbers compared to warm? ballpark?
[00:12:20] Mateo: cold first-token could be 2x or more of warm in some workloads, especially for long contexts; for short prefixes difference might be 20-50ms. exact numbers depend on model and cache hit rates.
[00:12:32] Ethan: will you help tune batcher parameters?
[00:12:35] Mateo: yes SEs typically tune max-batch-size, max-wait-ms, and priority lanes during onboarding. we can do that as part of the pilot.
[00:12:43] Priya: ok let's sketch the pilot flow: we run your bench config against hosted and provision a small dedicated pool, route 5% traffic for 2 weeks, collect p95 and quality, then decide.
[00:12:54] Lena: sounds solid. we'll include comparison templates for p95, token cost, and quality metrics.
[00:12:59] Samir: would Redwood sign an NDA? we need some IP-level details shared in the bench.
[00:13:05] Lena: yes we have an NDA template and a security addendum.
[00:13:09] Priya: any gotchas we should be aware of for streaming SSE vs Websocket?
[00:13:13] Mateo: websockets reduce connection overhead and are usually steadier for high concurrency; SSE is simpler but can be limited by proxies. we'll recommend websocket if you have heavy sustained sessions.
[00:13:24] Ethan: last technical: how do you measure per-token cost? are you including decode compute + KV access?
[00:13:29] Mateo: cost model factors GPU compute time, memory usage (KV affects memory but not always linearly), and any overhead from routing; the per-token metric we provide is normalized to tokens/sec * latency and we can show token-cost curves.
[00:13:41] (brief pause)
[00:13:55] Lena: ok moving towards wrap — recap: Redwoods action items — send benchmark config, SLA template, security docs; proposed next meeting to review bench results and Dedicated sizing. Customer actions — share token traces, sample prompts, and confirm pilot dates.
[00:14:10] Priya: agreed, we'll try to get traces today.
[00:14:14] Ethan: 1 more practical — do you offer sample load drivers or can we use your synthetic scripts?
[00:14:19] Mateo: we'll share our bench driver (node/python) and a config transforming your traces into bench scenarios.
[00:14:25] Jin: network emulation script too please.
[00:14:28] Mateo: will include.
[00:14:33] Asha: I'll own the security docs send and NDA.
[00:14:36] Lena: great. we'll target sending first set of materials by 2025-10-20 and a follow-up bench review the week of 2025-10-27.
[00:14:45] Samir: thanks all.
[00:14:46] (meeting continues with clarifying Qs about prompt formatting and sample deck references, audio drops occasionally)
[00:20:12] Ethan: sample prompt 12 tends to cause longer tail tokens, we can mark those as special cases in the bench.
[00:23:50] Mateo: we'll parameterize tail-heavy prompts and run them as a separate test.
[00:29:05] Priya: question on routing policies — can we pin a specific customer segment to Dedicated while others use hosted?
[00:29:12] Lena: yes, policy-based routing supports per-tenant pinning and header-based selection.
[00:33:44] Jin: I'm concerned about egress IP churn for hosted — if you can't pin IPs reliably we'll have to go Dedicated.
[00:33:50] Asha: noted, we'll include IP stability notes.
[00:38:02] Mateo: small note on metrics — we'll provide p50/p95/p99 and token-per-second heatmaps by minute to help you size.
[00:42:18] Priya: ok if you can also annotate quality regressions in the bench we'll be happy.
[00:42:23] Lena: yes canary A/B hooks available.
[00:47:00] (closing)
[00:57:30] Lena: thanks everyone, we'll send the materials and set the follow-up.
